question.text:
In a garden, $60\%$ of the flowers are roses. Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, approximate the probability that if $100$ flowers are picked at random, then $70$ of them will be roses. Give your answer to three decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.02 \,$$\, 0.03 \,$$\, 0.04 \,$
$\, 1.9 \,$ $\, 0.9726 \,$ $\, 0.9732 \,$ $\, 0.9738 \,$
$\, 2.0 \,$ $\, 0.9783 \,$ $\, 0.9788 \,$ $\, 0.9793 \,$
$\, 2.1 \,$ $\, 0.9830 \,$ $\, 0.9834 \,$ $\, 0.9838 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p = 0.6.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 100\cdot 0.6\\[5pt] &= 60 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 100\cdot (1-0.6) \\[5pt] &=40 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (100)(0.6) = 60 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (100)(0.6)(1-0.6) = 24. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(60, 24).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X = 70).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X = 70) \approx P(69.5 \leq Y \leq 70.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(69.5 \leq Y \leq 70.5) &= P \left( \dfrac{69.5-60}{\sqrt{24}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{70.5-60}{\sqrt{24}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( 1.94 \leq Z \leq 2.14 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq 2.14) - P(Z < 1.94) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq 2.14) - P(Z \leq 1.94) \\[5pt] &= \Phi(2.14) - \Phi(1.94) \\[5pt] &= 0.9838 - 0.9738 \\[5pt] &= 0.010 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(X = 70)\approx 0.010. \]

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0102.$

question.text:
In a music program at a college, an average of $45\%$ of graduating students go on to pursue a career in music. Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that in a graduating class of $200$ students, at least $110$ students will go on to pursue a career in music. Give your final answer to $3$ decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.05 \,$$\, 0.06 \,$$\, 0.07 \,$
$\, 2.6 \,$ $\, 0.9960 \,$ $\, 0.9961 \,$ $\, 0.9962 \,$
$\, 2.7 \,$ $\, 0.9970 \,$ $\, 0.9971 \,$ $\, 0.9972 \,$
$\, 2.8 \,$ $\, 0.9978 \,$ $\, 0.9979 \,$ $\, 0.9979 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=200$ and $p = 0.45.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 200\cdot 0.45\\[5pt] &= 90 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 200\cdot (1-0.45) \\[5pt] &=110 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*}

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (200)(0.45) = 90 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (200)(0.45)(1-0.45) = 49.5. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(90, 49.5).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X \geq 110).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X \geq 110) \approx P(Y > 109.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(Y > 109.5) &= 1 - P(Y \leq 109.5) \\[5pt] &= 1 - P \left( Z \leq \dfrac{109.5 - 90}{ \sqrt{49.5} } \right) \\[5pt] &\approx 1 - P(Z \leq 2.77) \\[5pt] &= 1 - \Phi( 2.77) \\[5pt] &=1-0.9972 \\[5pt] &=0.0028 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(X \geq 110) \approx 0.003. \] Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0028.$

example.title: Using a Normal Approximation to Approximate a Binomial Probability Over an Interval

question.text:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

  1. The probability that $5$ flights out of $50$ arrive late at an airport if the probability of arriving late is $0.09$ for each flight.
  2. The probability that a student correctly solves $3$ questions in a $5$-question math test if the student has a $46\%$ probability of correctly answering each question.
  3. The probability that a biased coin lands on heads more than $30$ times out of $80$ coin flips if the probability of a single flip landing on heads is $0.52.$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have $n=50$ and $p=0.09.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 50\cdot 0.09\\[5pt] &= 4.5\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation II, we have $n=5$ and $p=0.46.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 5\cdot 0.46\\[5pt] &= 2.3\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation III, we have $n=80$ and $p=0.52.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 80\cdot 0.52\\[5pt] &=41.6\\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 80\cdot (1-0.52) \\[5pt] &=38.4 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

example.title: Identifying Situations Where a Normal Approximation is Appropriate

question.text:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

  1. The probability of getting $48$ even numbers on $100$ rolls of a $6$-sided die.
  2. The probability that less than $4$ wireless earphones are defective from a box containing $30$ pairs of earphones if the probability of a single pair being defective is $0.15.$
  3. The probability that a basketball player scores $8$ of $20$ three-point shots if the probability of scoring each shot is $0.53.$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Let's now examine each situation.

  • In situation I, we have $n=100$ and $p=\dfrac16.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 100\cdot \dfrac{1}{6}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{50}{3} \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 100\cdot \left(1-\dfrac{1}{6}\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{250}{3} \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation II, we have $n=30$ and $p=0.15.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 30\cdot 0.15\\[5pt] &= 4.5\\[5pt] &\ngtr 5.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}\\[5pt] \end{align*} So, we cannot use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

  • In situation III, we have $n=20$ and $p=0.53.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 20\cdot 0.53\\[5pt] &= 10.6 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 20\cdot (1-0.53) \\[5pt] &=9.4 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

question.text:
Given that the random variable $X\sim B(165,0.6),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=90).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.

$z$$\, 0.00 \,$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$
$\, -1.5 \,$ $\, 0.0668 \,$ $\, 0.0655 \,$ $\, 0.0643 \,$
$\, -1.4 \,$ $\, 0.0808 \,$ $\, 0.0793 \,$ $\, 0.0778 \,$
$\, -1.3 \,$ $\, 0.0968 \,$ $\, 0.0951 \,$ $\, 0.0934 \,$
$z$$\, 0.05 \,$$\, 0.06 \,$$\, 0.07 \,$
$\, -1.5 \,$ $\, 0.0606 \,$ $\, 0.0594 \,$ $\, 0.0582 \,$
$\, -1.4 \,$ $\, 0.0735 \,$ $\, 0.0722 \,$ $\, 0.0708 \,$
$\, -1.3 \,$ $\, 0.0885 \,$ $\, 0.0869 \,$ $\, 0.0854 \,$
question.explanation:
Given a binomial random variable $X \sim B(n,p),$ if

  • $np > 5,$ and

  • $n(1-p) > 5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu = np$ and variance $\sigma^2 = np(1-p),$ that is,

\[ Y \sim N(np, np(1-p)). \]

Here, we have $n=165$ and $p = 0.6.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} np &= 165\cdot 0.6\\[5pt] &= 99 \\[5pt] &> 5\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}\\[10pt] n(1-p) &= 165\cdot (1-0.6) \\[5pt] &=66 \\[5pt] &> 5. \quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}} \end{align*} So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

\[ \mu = np = (165)(0.6) = 99 \]

and variance

\[ \sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (165)(0.6)(1-0.6) = 39.6. \]

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \sim N(99, 39.6).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X = 90).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

\[ P(X = 90) \approx P(89.5 \leq Y \leq 90.5). \]

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

\[ \begin{align*} P(89.5 \leq Y \leq 90.5) &= P \left( \dfrac{89.5-99}{\sqrt{39.6}} \leq Z \leq \dfrac{90.5-99}{\sqrt{39.6}} \right) \\[5pt] &\approx P \left( -1.51 \leq Z \leq -1.35 \right) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq -1.35) - P(Z < -1.51) \\[5pt] &= P(Z \leq -1.35) - P(Z \leq -1.51) \\[5pt] &= \Phi(-1.35) - \Phi(-1.51) \\[5pt] &=0.0885 - 0.0655 \\[5pt] &=0.023 \end{align*} \]

Therefore,

\[ P(X = 90)\approx 0.023. \]

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0227.$
